C1.note: Main results are polynomial-time algorithms for bribery problems (strategic action of an external briber posed as a computational problem).

C2.2.note: Strict orders; additionally restricted to single-peaked or single-crossing domains.

C2.3.quote: to the least appealing one for a given voter
C2.3.note: The paper refers to voters' preferences (what is appealing to a voter), but defines them as the vote itself; no separate object. Coded Y because preferences are attributed to voters, borderline with N.

C2.4.quote: under the Borda rule when voters’ preferences are single-peaked
C2.4.note: Votes are defined as voters' preference orders and the rule is applied to them directly; no statement about submission or reporting. Bribery is described as shifting p 'in their preferences'.

C3.1.quote: we can pay the voters to shift p forward in their rankings
C3.1.note: Bribery changes voters' rankings (framed as changing preferences, campaign management, or a measure of success); no analysis models a voter submitting an input different from a held attitude. Doubt: under the 'actual bribery' reading, bribed votes might differ from held preferences, but the paper never distinguishes them.

C4.1.quote: price of shifting the preferred candidate by s positions
C4.1.note: Applicability triggered strictly by the term 'cost', which here denotes bribery prices paid by the briber, not a voter utility notion. Price functions are defined as functions of how far p is shifted in each vote. No utility, welfare or satisfaction notions appear. If 'cost' is meant only as voter cost, this should be NA.

C4.2.note: The term dichotomous preferences is not used.

C5.1.note: Claims concern candidates' performance (measure of success) and complexity, not welfare or voters.

VOT.quote_behav: a collection of votes that rank the candidates
VOT.note: Votes are given as input and changed only by the briber's paid shifts; voters do not choose actions.

CAN.note: Candidates take no action in the formal model. In the motivating example the candidate (Claire) reasons about improving her position, and the paper says bribery models her reasoning, so the briber may be read as the candidate in the measure-of-success interpretation.

BRI.quote_behav: however, we would like to minimize the total expenditure
BRI.quote_info: In the R Shift Bribery problem we are given an election
BRI.note: Briber minimises cost subject to making p a winner; the full election, axis or voter order, and price functions are inputs to the problem. In the measure-of-success interpretation no actual bribery takes place.

C7.1.quote: to ensure that p is a winner of this election
C7.1.note: BRI is STRAT; VOT (and CAN) are NONSTRAT in the same analyses.
